prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay explaining how public-key cryptography works
raw:
I once spent three days teaching my mother to send me encrypted email about her surprise party for my father, only to watch her scrawl the passphrase on a Post-it note and stick it to the monitor. That was twenty years ago, and I still feel the sting of that little yellow square of failure. It taught me something crucial: public-key cryptography isn’t actually about math. It’s about the end of trust as we knew it, and frankly, we still haven’t adjusted to the new world.

Here is the thesis that your computer science professor will hate: the mathematical mechanism matters less than the cultural shift. When Diffie, Hellman, and Merkle published their work in 1976, they weren’t just proposing a clever way to exchange keys over a wire. They were proposing that two strangers could share a secret without ever meeting, without trusting a king or a priest or a banker to vouchsafe their communication. That idea was heretical. It still is.

The mechanics themselves are almost embarrassingly simple once you stop thinking about ciphers and start thinking about paint. Imagine I have a private color—let’s say it’s a particular shade of cadmium yellow that only I know. You have your own private color. We agree on a common color, say, Prussian blue, that everyone can see. Here’s the trick: mixing paint is one-way. You can pour blue and yellow together to get green, but you cannot unmix green into blue and yellow without a chemistry lab and a gas chromatograph.

So I send you my blue-and-yellow mixture. You send me your blue-and-your-secret mixture. I add my yellow to your mixture; you add your secret to my mixture. We both end up with the same three-color blend, identical to the drop, even though neither of us ever sent our pure secret through the mail. An eavesdropper sees the blue, sees the mixtures, sees the final shared green, but cannot work backward to isolate my yellow or your red. This is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, modulo some modular arithmetic that computers handle better than I do. The "paint" is usually a number raised to a power modulo a massive prime, but the intuition is identical: some operations are trivial to perform and brutally hard to reverse.

RSA, which Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman published a year later, takes this asymmetry further. Instead of just mixing secrets, it creates a pair of keys that function like a mailbox slot and the only key to the box. I can hand out padlocks—my public key—to anyone on the street. Anyone can snap a message inside a box and lock it shut, but only I hold the key that opens it. The mathematics rely on the fact that multiplying two enormous prime numbers is fast, but working backward from the product to find those factors is, for all practical purposes, impossible. We’re talking about numbers hundreds of digits long. Even with every computer on Earth working until the sun burns out, you won’t factor a 2048-bit RSA modulus by brute force.

But here is where I get cranky. We talk about "public" keys as if they were posted on a bulletin board, but in practice, they live in files with names like `id_rsa.pub`, sitting in directories that—if you’re running OpenSSH—have permissions set to 644. That.pub on the end matters. That’s the part you give away. The `id_rsa` part, the private key, stays locked at 600, readable only by you. I have spent too many Tuesday afternoons debugging why a deployment script couldn’t connect to a server, only to find that someone had copied both files to a laptop and forgotten that the private key travels with the same vulnerability as a skeleton key. The math is perfect. The implementation is a horror show of human error.

This is why key management—not the cryptography—keeps me up at night. The Discrete Log Problem or Integer Factorization might hold for another fifty years, or quantum computers might eat them for breakfast next decade, but right now, your private key is sitting in a `.pem` file on a CI/CD server with a password of "password123." I’ve seen it. I’ve helped clean up after it. We’ve built this cathedral of mathematical rigor—elliptic curves now, which use even smaller keys for the same security, based on the difficulty of finding points on a curve—and then we leave the blueprints taped to the front door.

What fascinates me most is the inversion of authority. Before 1975, if you wanted to keep a secret, you needed a courier with a locked briefcase handcuffed to his wrist, or you needed a diplomatic pouch. You needed infrastructure. You needed a state. Public-key cryptography turned that inside out. Suddenly, a dissident in Belarus could whisper a truth to a journalist in Oslo without asking Lukashenko’s permission or trusting the post office. The "public" in public key is a radical democratic act. It says: I don’t need your permission to be private.

We’re living through the consequences now, watching governments panic over iPhones they cannot crack and Signal protocols that leave no logs. They call it "going dark," as if mathematics were a curtain they could order torn down. But you cannot outlaw a field of algebra any more than you can outlaw the tide.

My mother never did master the art of key generation. She still writes passwords on sticky notes. But last week, she sent me a WhatsApp message about Dad’s birthday, and somewhere beneath that gray text bubble, her phone and mine performed a three-way handshake using Curve25519, generating a shared secret that she never saw, never wrote down, and never had to understand. The mathematics has become invisible, which is exactly what the good professors intended. We just have to make sure we don’t lose the keys to the kingdom while we’re busy staring at the locks.
